confidence_note: Written from knowledge of Unbroken; no page-level check. Core: Louis Zamperini, 1936 Olympian, bombardier; B-24 crashed in the Pacific in May 1943; three of eleven survived; Francis McNamara died during the drift; Zamperini and pilot Russell Phillips drifted 47 days on a raft, caught birds and fish and drank rain, then were captured by Japanese forces. The forgiveness visit in 1950 Sugamo prison is the book's account; kept only as the end. Omitted on purpose: McNamara's exact day, distances, shark details, names of camp guards, the Bird's name beyond 'a guard nicknamed the Bird', conversion details. Added from memory of Hillenbrand, not page-checked: crash on a search mission, eight died, day-33 death, 2,000 miles, strafing, family notified. Prison visit kept to the book's gist.
facts: Louis Zamperini ran at the 1936 Olympics and later served as a bombardier in the Second World War.
In May 1943 his bomber crashed in the Pacific; of eleven on board, three survived.
Zamperini, pilot Russell Phillips and a third man drifted on small rafts; the third man died during the drift.
The two survivors lived on rain water, fish and birds they caught, and drifted for 47 days before reaching land held by Japan.
They were taken prisoner; Zamperini spent about two years in prison camps, where a guard nicknamed the Bird tormented him.
After the war he came home angry and struggled; in 1950 he went to a prison in Tokyo and met former guards, as the book describes.
Zamperini ran the 5000 m in Berlin; the B-24 went down on a search mission; eight died in the crash; the third raft man died about day 33.
They covered roughly two thousand miles; sharks circled; a Japanese plane strafed the raft; the Bird picked him out because he was a famous athlete; his family had been told he was dead.
scene_details: a rain-water ration on a small raft
a prison visit in Tokyo in 1950
tension: A man survives 47 days at sea and two years of camps, and the harder part comes at home.
opening_idea: Open on the raft: two men, 47 days, rain water, fish and birds.

lessons.idea: Surviving a hardship is not the same as being free of it; the resentment you carry is a separate task.
lessons.anchor: Zamperini came home angry after the camps

reflect_final: Which old grievance still takes your attention, and what small step toward putting it down could you take this month?

pocket_idea: Zamperini survived the raft and the camps, then had to deal with anger: staying alive is not the same as being free.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Zamperini survived 47 days on a raft, and the war was still following him home.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Louis Zamperini, an Olympic runner, survived a Pacific bomber crash and 47 days adrift on a raft before being taken prisoner by Japanese forces. He lived through about two years of camps, where a guard called the Bird targeted him. Back home he was full of anger. In 1950 he went to a prison in Tokyo to meet former guards. Laura Hillenbrand tells this in Unbroken.
